subject: Archaeology
title: Decolonizing Archaeology
description: A micro-lesson that makes Decolonizing Archaeology usable.

hook.text: Archaeology was born during colonialism. Its founders shipped heritage to European museums.

buildup.text: Western scholars told African and Indigenous stories for decades — often wrongly.

discovery.text: Decolonizing means centering local voices and sharing authority with communities.

twist.text: Museum boards, journal editors, and funding panels remain overwhelmingly Western.

climax.text: New programs fund Global South researchers and build community-owned projects.

punchline.text: Archaeology studied every past except its own. Now it looks in the mirror.

quiz.question: What does decolonizing archaeology involve?
options: Stopping all work in formerly colonized nations
Centering local voices and sharing authority with communities
Returning every artifact to its origin country

details.summary: Decolonizing archaeology means confronting the discipline's roots in colonialism — when European powers excavated foreign sites, shipped artifacts home, and interpreted other cultures through Western frameworks.
details.whyItMatters: Archaeology was born during the colonial era and carries its legacy. Decolonization is not just about returning objects — it requires rethinking whose knowledge counts, who tells the stories, and who benefits from research.
takeaways: Archaeology's origins are intertwined with European colonialism
Decolonization centers local voices and returns stolen artifacts
It challenges Western interpretive frameworks applied globally

faq.question: What does decolonizing archaeology look like in practice?
faq.answer: It involves training and employing local archaeologists, publishing in local languages, sharing data openly, returning artifacts, seeking community consent before excavation, and incorporating indigenous knowledge systems alongside Western scientific methods.

faq.question: Why is repatriation of artifacts a decolonization issue?
faq.answer: Colonial-era excavations removed millions of objects without consent. Major museums hold collections that source countries want returned. The debate centers on whether universal museums serve global knowledge or perpetuate colonial power by keeping stolen cultural heritage.
